topics.title: Arcs and angles at the centre

inlines.text: applies deductive reasoning to prove circle theorems and solve related problems
Prove and apply angle and chord properties of circles
Apply terminology associated with angles in circles
Identify the arc on which an angle at the centre or circumference stands
Demonstrate that at any point on a circle there is a unique tangent to the circle, and that this tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact
Apply chord and angle properties of circles to find unknown angles and lengths in diagrams
Prove and apply tangent and secant properties of circles
Prove tangent and secant properties of circles
Apply tangent and secant properties of circles to find unknown angles and lengths in diagrams
The circumference of a circle is the perimeter, or distance around the outside of a circle.
An arc is a part of the circumference.
All points on the circumference are the same distance from the centre.
A circle is the set of all points an equal distance from the centre.
A tangent is a straight line that touches the circumference at a single point without entering the circle.
A chord is a straight line segment that goes from one point on the circumference to another point.

The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord:

$$\begin{align*}XZ &= \frac{8}{2}\\ &= 4\text{ cm}.\end{align*}$$

In the isosceles triangle $XOY$, $OZ$ also bisects the angle at $O$:

$$\begin{align*}\angle XOZ &= \frac{102^\circ}{2}\\ &= 51^\circ.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
In this diagram, radius $AD=5\text{ mm}$, radius $BD=12\text{ mm}$ and chord $CD=8\text{ mm}$.
Find the exact length of $AB$, in surd form.

spec.description: Smaller circle centred at A on the left and larger circle centred at B on the right. C and D are their upper and lower intersections. Solid line AB crosses dashed common chord CD; all four radii to the intersections are dashed.
spec.mathematics: AD = AC = 5 mm; BD = BC = 12 mm; CD = 8 mm. The centres lie on opposite sides of the common chord. Coordinates derive from half-chord 4 mm, with distances 3 mm and 8√2 mm from the common chord.
spec.answerVisibility: The diagram contains only the source labels A, B, C and D. No numerical result or added midpoint label appears.

answer.worked:
Let $M$ be the intersection of $AB$ and $CD$. The line joining the centres bisects the common chord at right angles, so $DM=4\text{ mm}$.
$$\begin{aligned}AM^2&=AD^2-DM^2\\AM^2&=5^2-4^2=9\\AM&=3\text{ mm}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}BM^2&=BD^2-DM^2\\BM^2&=12^2-4^2=128\\BM&=8\sqrt{2}\text{ mm}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}AB&=AM+BM\\AB&=(3+8\sqrt{2})\text{ mm}\end{aligned}$$

answer.worked:
In $\triangle OAP$ and $\triangle OBP$:

$$\begin{aligned}\angle OPA&=\angle OPB=90^\circ\\OA&=OB\end{aligned}$$

The angles are right angles because $OP\perp AB$, and $OA=OB$ because they are radii. Also $OP$ is common.

answer.worked:
Construct $BC$ and join $OB$ and $OC$.

answer.worked:
$AD=BD$ (radii of the circle with centre $D$).

$AC=BC$ (radii of the circle with centre $C$).

$CD$ is common.

Therefore, $\triangle ACD\cong\triangle BCD$ (SSS).

$AC=BC$ (radii).

$\angle ACE=\angle BCE$ (corresponding angles in the congruent triangles from part a, since $C,E,D$ are collinear).

$CE$ is common.

Therefore, $\triangle ACE\cong\triangle BCE$ (SAS).

$\angle BEC=\angle CEA$ (corresponding angles in the congruent triangles from part b).

These angles lie on the straight line $AB$, so each is $90^\circ$. Therefore, $CD\perp AB$.

Also, $BE=EA$ (corresponding sides in $\triangle ACE\cong\triangle BCE$).

answer.short: Base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal (equal radii); $\angle OAC$; $\angle OCA$; $x+y$.
answer.worked:
Since $OA=OC$, the base angles of $\triangle AOC$ are equal.
$$\begin{align*}\angle OAC&=\angle OCA=x\\\angle POA&=\angle OAC+\angle OCA\\\angle POA&=2x\end{align*}$$
Similarly, $OB=OC$ gives $\angle POB=2y$ by the exterior-angle property.
$$\begin{align*}\angle AOB&=2x+2y\\\angle AOB&=2(x+y)\\\angle AOB&=2\times\angle ACB\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Centre outside angle ACB; dashed diameter POC, equal-radius double ticks, x between CA and CO and y spanning CO to CB.
spec.mathematics: OA=OB; P,O,C are collinear. Angle ACB=y-x; y is the entire angle OCB.
spec.answerVisibility: No completed proof or derived angle values.

answer.worked:
Equal radii give equal base angles in $\triangle AOC$ and $\triangle BOC$. By the exterior-angle property,
$$\begin{align*}\angle POA&=x+x\\\angle POA&=2x\\\angle POB&=y+y\\\angle POB&=2y\\\angle AOB&=\angle POB-\angle POA\\\angle AOB&=2y-2x\\\angle AOB&=2(y-x)\end{align*}$$
At $C$, $\angle ACB=y-x$. Therefore $\angle AOB=2\times\angle ACB$.

answer.short: $\angle OCB=90^\circ-x$; base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal; $\angle COB=2x$; $\angle BAC=x$.
answer.worked:
Join $CO$ and $BO$. Let $\angle BCQ=x$.

$\angle OCB=90^\circ-x$ because $OC$ is perpendicular to the tangent.

$OB=OC$, so $\angle OBC=90^\circ-x$ because base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal.

$$\begin{aligned}\angle COB&=180^\circ-(90^\circ-x)-(90^\circ-x)\\\angle COB&=2x\end{aligned}$$

The angle at the centre is double the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc:

$$\begin{aligned}\angle BAC&=\frac{2x}{2}\\\angle BAC&=x\end{aligned}$$

Therefore $\angle BCQ=\angle CAB$.

content.prompt:
The diagram shows quadrilateral $ABCD$ and the bisectors of the angles at $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$. The bisectors at $A$ and $B$ intersect at the point $P$. The bisectors at $A$ and $D$ meet at $Q$. The bisectors at $C$ and $D$ meet at $R$. The bisectors at $B$ and $C$ meet at $S$.

Show that $PQRS$ is a cyclic quadrilateral.

spec.description: Quadrilateral and its four angle bisectors, with Q below BC and the inner quadrilateral emphasised.
spec.mathematics: P=AP∩BP, Q=AQ∩DQ, R=CR∩DR, S=BS∩CS; each vertex angle has two equal labelled halves.
spec.answerVisibility: All supplied angle-half labels are permanent givens; the proof is answer-only.

answer.worked:
Let $\alpha=\frac12\angle A$, $\beta=\frac12\angle B$, $\gamma=\frac12\angle C$ and $\delta=\frac12\angle D$.

The angle sum of quadrilateral $ABCD$ gives
$$\begin{align*}2\alpha+2\beta+2\gamma+2\delta&=360^\circ\\\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta&=180^\circ.\end{align*}$$
Using the angle sums of $\triangle BSC$ and $\triangle AQD$,
$$\begin{align*}\angle PSR&=\angle BSC=180^\circ-(\beta+\gamma)\\\angle PQR&=\angle AQD=180^\circ-(\alpha+\delta).\end{align*}$$
Here $SP$ lies along $SB$ and $SR$ lies along $SC$, while $QP$ lies along $QA$ and $QR$ lies along $QD$.
$$\begin{align*}\angle PSR+\angle PQR&=2\times180^\circ-(\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta)\\\angle PSR+\angle PQR&=2\times180^\circ-180^\circ\\\angle PSR+\angle PQR&=180^\circ.\end{align*}$$
Therefore $PQRS$ is cyclic because its opposite angles are supplementary.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\angle ADB&=90^\circ\\\angle BCA&=90^\circ\end{align*}$$
Both are angles in a semicircle. Since $DB$ and $DM$ are opposite rays, and $DE$ lies along $DA$,
$$\angle MDE=180^\circ-\angle ADB=90^\circ.$$
Thus exterior $\angle ACB$ equals opposite interior $\angle MDE$, so $CMDE$ is cyclic.

answer.worked:
Construct $CD$. Let $\angle ABC=x$.

Angles standing on chord $AC$ give $\angle ADC=x$. Since $D,E,A$ are collinear, $\angle EDC=x$. In cyclic quadrilateral $CMDE$, angles standing on chord $CE$ give $\angle CME=\angle CDE=x$.

In $\triangle ABC$, $\angle BCA=90^\circ$, so
$$\angle CAB=90^\circ-x.$$
Since $MC$ lies along $MA$ and $ME$ lies along $MF$, the angle sum of $\triangle MFA$ gives
$$\begin{align*}\angle MFA&=180^\circ-\angle CME-\angle CAB\\\angle MFA&=180^\circ-x-(90^\circ-x)\\\angle MFA&=90^\circ.\end{align*}$$
Therefore $MF\perp AB$.

Construct $OC$, $AC$ and $OQ$. Let $\angle BPC=\phi$.

Since $BP=BC$, $\triangle BPC$ is isosceles, so $\angle BCP=\phi$. The exterior angle at $B$ gives $\angle OBC=2\phi$.

By the alternate segment theorem, $\angle BAC=\angle BCP=\phi$. Since $AB$ is a diameter, $\angle BCA=90^\circ$.
$$\begin{align*}\phi+2\phi&=90^\circ\\\phi&=30^\circ.\end{align*}$$
The radius is perpendicular to the tangent, so $OA\perp AQ$ and
$$\angle CAQ=90^\circ-\phi=60^\circ.$$
Tangents from $Q$ are equal: $QA=QC$. Thus $\triangle QAC$ is isosceles and $\angle QCA=60^\circ$. Hence
$$\angle AQC=180^\circ-60^\circ-60^\circ=60^\circ.$$
Triangles $OAQ$ and $OCQ$ are congruent by SSS: $OA=OC$ (radii), $AQ=CQ$ (equal tangents), and $OQ$ is common. Therefore $OQ$ bisects $\angle AQC$, giving
$$\angle OQC=\frac{60^\circ}{2}=30^\circ=\angle OPC.$$
Since $P,C,Q$ are collinear, $\angle OQP=\angle OQC$ and $\angle OPQ=\angle OPC$. Thus $\triangle OPQ$ is isosceles and $OP=OQ$.

entries.description:
The circle centred at O has diameter AB. A point P on AB produced is chosen so that PC is a tangent to the circle at C and BP = BC. The tangents to the circle at A and C meet at Q.
Prove that OP = OQ.

entries.expectedAnswer: A proof that OP = OQ; supplied source proof recorded separately.

entries.description: Circle with centre O, C at its bottom, B on the lower-left circumference and A on the upper-right circumference. P, B, O and A are collinear in that order. P, C and Q lie on the horizontal tangent at C, with P left and Q right. The tangent at A meets this line at Q and extends beyond A. Drawn segments include AB, BC, OC, AC, OQ, PQ and AQ. All point labels P, B, O, A, C, Q are visible. Single ticks mark OB, OA and OC; double ticks mark PB and BC; triple ticks mark AQ and CQ. Solution annotations show φ at ∠BPC, φ at ∠BCP, 2φ at ∠OBC, φ at ∠BAC, and a right-angle marker at ∠BCA.

presentation.authoring: Editable free-form TikZ; black geometry and ordinary labels at 10 pt; no shading.
presentation.orientation: Preserve point order, diameter, tangent contacts and intersections.
presentation.studentGivens: Centre O; diameter AB; P on AB produced beyond B; PC tangent at C; BP = BC; tangents at A and C meeting at Q.
presentation.answerOnlyAnnotations: Constructed OC, AC and OQ; φ and 2φ angle annotations; derived right angle at C; equality marks for AQ and CQ.

entries.description: Supplied blue worked proof beneath the diagram.
entries.expectedAnswer:
Construct OC, AC, OQ.
Let ∠BPC have size φ.
△BPC is isosceles so ∠BCP is φ.
∠OBC is an external angle, so ∠OBC = 2φ.
∠BAC is angle on chord BC, so ∠BAC = φ (angle in alternate segment and angle between chord and tangent).
But △BAC has a right angle at C (angle in semicircle).
So φ + 2φ = 90°, hence φ = 30°.
OA ⟂ AQ (angle between tangent and radius).
So ∠CAQ = 60°.
QA = QC (tangents from point equal).
So ∠QCA = 60° (△QAC isosceles).
Hence ∠AQC = 60° (angle sum of triangle).
△OAQ and △OCQ are congruent (SSS: OA = OC, radii; AQ = CQ, above; OQ common).
So ∠OQC = 60°/2 = 30° = ∠OPC.
Thus △OPQ is isosceles, and OP = OQ.

presentation.answerPlacement: Worked-answer edition only; keep supplied proof and derived diagram annotations out of the student prompt.
presentation.taughtMethods: Isosceles triangles, exterior angle, alternate segment theorem, angle in a semicircle, tangent-radius perpendicularity, equal tangents, triangle angle sum and SSS congruence.
